title: Paired vagus nerve stimulation therapy for posterior circulation ischemic strokes: illustrative cases.
abstract: While the global disability burden due to stroke remains substantial, the emergence of novel neurorestorative therapies offers new opportunities for poststroke recovery. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) paired with upper extremity (UE) rehabilitation (paired VNS) is an FDA-approved therapy shown to improve UE impairment and reduce motor deficits in patients with chronic stroke. However, published evidence describing its use in posterior circulation strokes is limited. This case series presents 4 patients with persistent UE impairment following posterior fossa strokes who underwent implantation and treatment with paired VNS months to years after their cerebrovascular event. Functional improvements were observed in all cases, including gains in Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity or Wolf Motor Function Test scores. All patients also reported improved functional use of the affected limb during daily activities and improvements in their quality of life. These cases suggest that paired VNS therapy may support meaningful functional recovery following posterior fossa stroke, even years after the initial event. Improvements were observed in both objective motor outcomes and patient-reported function and quality of life. These observations expand the clinical experience with paired VNS in a stroke subpopulation associated with significant long-term disability, and contribute to addressing a gap in the literature. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26535.

title: Teaching NeuroImage: Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusion Disease Presenting With Both Macular and Higher Visual Dysfunction.
Sex Differences in Blood Pressure Dynamics and Outcomes After Endovascular Thrombectomy.
abstract: Optimal blood pressure (BP) management after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains controversial, and whether early BP dynamics differentially affect outcomes among female and male participants is unclear. This was an exploratory secondary analysis of ENCHANTED2/MT, a multicenter, open-label, blinded-end point randomized trial conducted in 44 tertiary hospitals in China. Eligible adults had AIS due to large-vessel occlusion, successful reperfusion after EVT, and persistent elevated systolic BP (SBP) within 3 hours after reperfusion. Serial BP measurements obtained during the first 72 hours after randomization were used to estimate patient-specific mean BP trajectories and short-term BP variability with a location-scale mixed-effects modeling approach. Associations of mean BP, BP variability, and randomized intensive vs standard BP lowering strategy with clinical outcomes were examined, with sex being evaluated as an effect modifier. The primary outcome was the 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Among 816 patients (mean age 67.6 ± 12.0 years; 38% female), intensive BP management was associated with worse 90-day ordinal mRS outcome among male participants (adjusted common odds ratio [acOR] 1.91; 95% CI 1.29-2.83), whereas the corresponding estimate among female participants was closer to null (acOR 0.94; 95% CI 0.56-1.57; ratio of acORs 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.94). In separate postrandomization BP exposure models, each 5 mm Hg higher mean SBP was associated with worse 90-day mRS outcome among male participants (acOR 1.11; 95% CI 1.03-1.20), whereas no clear adverse association was observed among female participants (acOR 0.95; 95% CI 0.85-1.05; ratio of acORs 0.85; 95% CI 0.75-0.97). SBP variability showed weaker and less consistent sex differential associations. Findings across secondary outcomes were directionally similar but exploratory. In this exploratory secondary analysis of ENCHANTED2/MT, randomized BP management strategy and early post-thrombectomy BP dynamics showed sex-stratified associations with outcomes. These associations may reflect biological sex and sex-related differences in baseline clinical and vascular characteristics. These findings are hypothesis generating and should be confirmed in prospectively designed studies before informing sex-specific BP management after EVT. ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04140110; the Registration Date, October 22, 2019.

title: Slipping Rib Syndrome as a Movement Disorder Mimic.
Clinical Reasoning: A 69-Year-Old Female Patient With Rapid-Onset Levodopa-Responsive Rest Tremor, Parkinsonism, and Gait Freezing.
abstract: The evaluation of rapid-onset parkinsonism can be challenging, and the differential diagnosis encompasses a broad spectrum of etiology, management, and prognosis. We present a 69-year-old patient who developed rapid-onset resting tremor and parkinsonism with gait freezing. Her upper limb resting tremor began unilaterally but rapidly progressed to involve the contralateral limb and subsequently the lower limbs. This evolved within 3 months to also include generalized parkinsonism and a shuffling gait with prominent freezing and frequent falls. Her tremor was levodopa responsive; however, other symptoms were resistant to treatment. Through this case, we will demonstrate the diagnostic approach to rapid-onset parkinsonism, summarizing a comprehensive evaluation of history, examination, and investigations. Readers will consider atypical features revealed by examination and investigations, ultimately arriving at a conclusive and critical diagnosis not to be missed in the presentation of parkinsonism.

title: Toward Personalized Sex-Informed Management of Blood Pressure After Stroke Thrombectomy Reperfusion.
Clinical Reasoning: A 33-Year-Old Man With Rapidly Progressive Ataxia.
abstract: Immunocompromised patients presenting with subacute neurologic deficits pose a diagnostic challenge given the broad differential diagnosis including infections and autoimmune disorders. We describe a 33-year-old man with AIDS who presented with subacute onset of progressive confusion, blurry vision, diplopia, and generalized cerebellar ataxia following hospitalizations for opportunistic infections. This case emphasizes the clinical and diagnostic approach used to refine the differential diagnosis of rhombencephalitis in an immunocompromised patient. Readers will gain an understanding of the various infectious, immunologic, and neoplastic etiologies to consider as well as the interplay between these pathologies.

title: A signal convention in natural chimpanzee communication.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Human language relies on conventional signals that are arbitrary, stable, and socially transmitted. Whether other animals exhibit meaning-based communicative conventions is virtually unknown. Using a quasi-experimental design, we investigated this in chimpanzee unvoiced calls (UCs), such as acoustic raspberries, known to show usage variation. We collected audio and contextual data in 91 chimpanzees (0 to 55 y), across eight wild and captive groups that differed in the presence or absence of adult role models. Communities with role models emitted UCs in one dominant context, which remained stable over years and from first utterances in development (1 to 2 y old). In contrast, groups without role models displayed highly variable, unstable UC usage across contexts and years. This contextual variation could not be explained by age or by a shared emotional valence, and individuals could use different UC forms within the same context, suggesting a decoupling between the signal form and usage. Together, these findings provide evidence that chimpanzee UCs meet key criteria for a signal convention: arbitrary signal-usage mappings, social transmission, and stability within communities. These findings demonstrate that conventionalized communication is not a uniquely human feature but can also emerge through social learning mechanisms in other animals' natural communication.

title: Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children ([Formula: see text]) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal Belief-contingent condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a "guess" (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on-Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.

title: The decision to stop "counting" explains numerical underproduction in primates.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Sequential numerical production requires generating a target number of actions, but the mechanisms governing the termination of counting sequences are unclear. We trained two rhesus macaques to produce instructed numerosities by generating the corresponding number of actions in response to sign numerals or dot arrays. Although action sequences were controlled for temporal parameters, both monkeys performed accurately across both stimulus formats. However, their performance accuracy showed a systematic asymmetry: underproduction occurred more often than overproduction, contrary to predictions from perceptual numerosity judgments governed by Weber-Fechner scaling. This asymmetry was mirrored in reaction times, with longer latencies for underproduced sequences and shorter latencies for overproduced ones. A stochastic accumulation-to-bound model in which a decision variable evolves across counting steps and triggers termination when a threshold is reached can account for both accuracy and reaction-time patterns. These results provide evidence for a sequential stopping process that contributes to numerical production, relating counting behavior to general principles of decision formation.

title: Exercise-Induced Changes in Cerebral Blood Flow as a Mechanism for Reducing Depression.
abstract: Late-life depression (LLD) is often caused or exacerbated by cerebrovascular pathology; whereas exercise has well-documented effects on improving cerebrovascular function, including cerebral blood flow (CBF). We propose that exercise may alleviate depressive symptoms and reduce LLD by enhancing CBF. However, this mechanistic pathway has not been directly tested. Future research should evaluate this model to develop targeted interventions for LLD. Summary: Exercise-induced changes in cerebral blood flow may mediate the association between exercise and depression in older adults.

title: Structure-Guided Design of a Selective Fluorogenic Probe for Monitoring Butyrylcholinesterase Activity in Living Cells.
journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
abstract: Butyrylcholinesterase (BuChE) is an important modulator of cholinergic signaling whose activity increases in several pathological contexts, including neurodegeneration and metabolic dysfunction. However, selective chemical tools for monitoring BuChE activity in complex biological systems remain limited, largely due to its high structural similarity to acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and the deeply buried nature of its catalytic site. Here, we report a series of activatable fluorescent probes based on a 1,8-naphthalimide scaffold for selective BuChE sensing. Probe performance was systematically optimized by varying ester substituents (cyclopropyl, cyclobutyl, cyclopentyl, and cyclohexyl) at the recognition site and by incorporating self-immolative linkers to spatially decouple the fluorophore from the enzymatic trigger. Among the probes developed, the cyclopropyl ester derivative JCB-3 exhibited superior performance, displaying high selectivity for BuChE over acetylcholinesterase (AChE), a low detection limit of 0.84 U/L, and a rapid fluorescence turn-on response within 20 min. Molecular docking studies supported the favorable binding of JCB-3 within the BuChE catalytic pocket. In live-cell imaging experiments, JCB-3 demonstrated excellent cell permeability, low cytotoxicity, and robust activation by endogenous BuChE. Together, these findings establish JCB-3 as a selective chemical probe for imaging BuChE activity and provide mechanistic insight into steric factors that govern cholinesterase selectivity.

title: Nuclear magnetic resonance therapy for deep-tissue biophysical stimulation: an integrated clinical and molecular analysis.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, radicular syndromes, and osteoporosis require noninvasive treatments reaching deep anatomical structures. Nuclear magnetic resonance therapy (NMRT/MBST) delivers depth-independent resonance-based stimulation. This systematic review consolidates clinical and mechanistic evidence to evaluate NMRT/MBST among deep-tissue biophysical therapeutics. A systematic search of PubMed, Ovid/Embase, and peer-reviewed literature identified 26 original studies spanning randomized and observational clinical evidence, imaging evaluations, veterinary trials, and in vitro research. Experimental findings on inflammatory, metabolic, mitochondrial, redox, and circadian pathways were integrated with clinical observations. NMRT/MBST shows a strong safety profile with no reported treatment-emergent adverse events. Across indications, studies demonstrate improvements in pain, function, and, selectively, structural or densitometric changes. Mechanistic evidence indicates modulation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox balance, inflammatory cascades, chondrogenic and osteogenic pathways, neurotrophic activity, and circadian regulation. These convergent processes mirror photobiomodulation, supporting NMRT/MBST as a deep-acting analog influencing regenerative biology in inaccessible tissues. Conventional pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is physically the closest comparator but shows narrower mechanistic overlap. Evidence remains heterogeneous in methodology, outcome measures, and structural responses. The only placebo-controlled knee osteoarthritis trial found no superiority over sham, although baseline imbalance limits interpretation. The depth-independent profile and mechanistic parallels suggest applications in deep cartilage, subchondral bone, intervertebral discs, and nerve-root environments, supporting multimodal biophysical strategies. Priorities include larger randomized trials, longitudinal structural evaluation, comparisons with optical modalities, and biomarker-guided personalization.

title: Protocol for whole-mount staining of melanized insect tissues for RNA and protein detection.
abstract: Technical barriers have limited whole-mount staining and imaging of internal tissues in many insects and other arthropods. Here, we present a protocol for whole-mount staining of melanized insect tissues for RNA and protein detection. We describe steps for preparing, permeabilizing, and bleaching samples; designing RNA probes; and staining. We then detail procedures for imaging samples. This protocol is compatible with both immunohistochemistry and fluorescence in situ hybridization and enables high-resolution microscopy of tissues surrounded by cuticle without sectioning. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Glotzer et al.1.
